name: Policosanol
short: One trial found reduced platelet aggregation, another did not; with beta-blockers, blood pressure fell more than on placebo. A pooled analysis judged it safer than control agents (effects not listed).
text: A meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials with 1886 participants concluded from its adverse effects analysis that sugarcane policosanol was safer than the control agents; the abstract does not list the adverse effects, and the authors noted high heterogeneity and that studies from Cuba reported larger treatment effects than studies elsewhere. Policosanol may affect platelets: in a 30-day placebo-controlled trial in healthy volunteers and patients with high cholesterol it moderately but significantly reduced platelet aggregation, whereas a crossover study in 12 healthy men, which also tested echinacea, found that 2 weeks of policosanol had no significant effect on platelet aggregation and did not significantly affect warfarin pharmacokinetics or the response to a single dose of warfarin. In a 3-year placebo-controlled trial in 205 older patients with high cholesterol who were taking beta-blockers, policosanol did not increase adverse events and serious adverse events were less frequent than with placebo (3.1% versus 14.0%), but systolic and diastolic blood pressure fell more than with placebo; the authors of that trial state that pharmacodynamic drug interactions cannot be excluded.
